title: Draught-sealing the conservatory-to-house threshold
subtitle: Stopping cold air moving between the conservatory and the main house
excerpt: The door between a conservatory and the main house is often the most draughty internal opening in the building. Sealing the frame, threshold, and glazing surround here cuts heat loss from the house and makes the conservatory usable as a buffer zone in winter.
sourceNotes: Energy Saving Trust guidance on conservatories and thermal performance; Building Regs Approved Document L2B on retrofits; field practice from Green Deal and ECO survey reports.

glossaryTerms.definition: Sealing strips applied around doors, windows, and openings to block cold air infiltration.
A path through a building element that conducts heat more readily than the surrounding insulation, causing localised cold spots and condensation risk.
The ability of a material to absorb and store heat energy, moderating temperature swings.

content.text: The door between a conservatory and the main house works harder than most external doors. It carries the full temperature difference between a heated room and an unheated glazed extension. Most of the heat loss comes from the frame perimeter, the threshold, and the glazing surround.

Sealing this threshold costs very little. It pays back within a single heating season. A well-sealed door turns the conservatory into a useful buffer zone. In winter, the conservatory air stays warmer than outside. This means the door already faces less temperature difference, even before the seal is fitted.
What you need to know first
Measure the door perimeter (frame rebate depth and width) before buying strips. Hinged doors typically need 9 to 12 mm compression foam or a rubber fin; sliding doors need a brush strip.

Check whether the door is a standard timber, uPVC, or aluminium frame. The adhesive on self-adhesive foam strips does not bond reliably to dirty or chalky surfaces. Clean with isopropyl alcohol first.
The threshold strip is the most exposed piece. Choose a rubber or aluminium threshold bar with a rubber wiper rather than a simple foam pad; it survives foot traffic where foam does not.
The draught-sealing sequence
Open the door fully and run your hand around the closed frame to find where cold air enters. Mark the gaps with masking tape.
Clean the rebate surfaces with a damp cloth and then isopropyl wipe. Allow to dry.
Press self-adhesive
draught stripping
into the rebate on the latch side and top first. Start from a corner; do not stretch the strip.
Cut the hinge-side strip to length with scissors or a craft knife. Press firmly for 30 seconds per 300 mm length.
Fit the threshold bar last. Screw the aluminium channel to the sill; thread in the rubber wiper; close the door and check the wiper makes contact along the full width.

Recheck the glazing surround: the junction between the glass unit and the frame can be an equal source of infiltration. Run a thin bead of low-modulus silicone around any open gaps and smooth with a wet finger.
The conservatory as a buffer zone
An unheated conservatory acts as a
thermal mass

buffer only if the door between it and the house is sealed. Cold air from a leaky threshold can circulate into a heated room and raise heating demand by 5 to 10% in a cold-facing glazed extension. Keeping the conservatory closed and unheated in winter uses the sun-warmed air in the space as insulation. A metal frame can also form a
cold bridge
at the wall junction.
What done well looks like

A well-sealed threshold has no visible gaps, the door closes with light resistance from the strip, and the threshold bar wipes cleanly across the full sill. Run your hand around the closed frame on a windy day; you should feel no movement.
What done badly looks like

Foam strip compressed completely flat. Threshold bar screwed down without the wiper touching. Gaps at corners where strips were measured short. Silicone applied over a dirty surface that peels away within a month.
Troubleshooter

rows.symptom: Door no longer closes fully after fitting foam strip
rows.cause: Strip is too thick for the rebate gap
rows.fix: Replace with a thinner strip (6 to 8 mm foam) or a rubber fin profile that compresses under less force.

rows.symptom: Cold draught still felt at the bottom of the door
rows.cause: Threshold bar wiper not reaching the full width of the sill, or threshold surface uneven
rows.fix: Re-seat the wiper; check the sill for warping and pack with a self-adhesive foam shim if the sill is bowed.

rows.symptom: Silicone around glazing shrinks and gaps reopen within a month
rows.cause: Low-quality silicone or applied to a dirty surface
rows.fix: Remove with a silicone remover tool, clean back to bare frame, and reapply a low-modulus neutral-cure silicone.
